clue.text: Oldster's greeting managed to shoo ducks away before two daughters come in

indicators.note: the two daughters come in, entering the word already built
shooing the ducks away drives the two Os out of the greeting, with the managing word taking their place
completes the shooing: the ducks are sent away from the greeting

parts.note: good day is a greeting
a duck is a zero in cricket, so two ducks are the letters O and O
managed means ran, as in ran a business
D is the abbreviation for daughter, so two of them give DD

explanation.surface: An old man says hello, then flaps his arms to scatter the ducks before his two daughters arrive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to shoo ... away' drives the two ducks out of the greeting and 'managed' takes their place; 'come in' then sets the daughters inside, before the last letter. The 's is a link ('is').
explanation.definitionFit: A granddaddy is an informal word for a grandfather, the archetypal elderly man, so it fits an oldster.

clue.text: Say 'Ah' maybe when doctor rings

indicators.note: the doctor's letters ring, surrounding the word for when

parts.note: a GP is a general practitioner, a family doctor
as can mean when, as in 'as I left'

explanation.surface: A patient told to say 'Ah' when the doctor phones.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say Ah' suggests the doctor's throat check, but 'Ah!' is an exclamation of surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: Uttering 'ah' in astonishment is a sharp intake of breath, a sound of surprise.

clue.text: Draw contents of dustcart, Tate putting it up

indicators.note: in a down clue, putting something up reads it from bottom to top, backwards
the letters are taken from inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A dustcart's contents displayed at the Tate gallery as art.
explanation.definitionFit: To draw a crowd is to pull it in, to entice people towards something.

clue.text: Cook had claret, messed up sweet

indicators.note: the letters of the three words are messed up into a new order

explanation.surface: A cook who had been drinking claret made a mess of the pudding.
explanation.definitionFit: A bar of bitter, cocoa-rich confectionery is a kind of sweet in British usage.

clue.text: Meeting subjects, aim to stay in range of country houses?

indicators.note: the aim stays inside the cooker's name

parts.note: an Aga is a cast-iron cooking range typical of British country house kitchens
an end is an aim or goal

explanation.surface: An attempt to stay in a stretch of country houses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'range' looks like a line of houses; it is the AGA cooker found in them.
explanation.definitionFit: The list of items to be discussed at a meeting is its programme of business.

clue.text: Explaining it's economically punishing to underwrite lower classes

indicators.note: to write underneath: in a down clue the punishing word goes below the classes

parts.note: D and E are the lowest UK social grades
fining is punishing with a money penalty

explanation.walkthrough: 'it's' is a link. UK marketing grades run A to E, D and E being the lowest.
explanation.definitionFit: Setting out a word's meaning precisely is giving its explanation, as a dictionary does.

clue.text: Golf and yet more golf — one's soundly beaten

parts.note: G is golf in the NATO phonetic alphabet
on means further, continuing, as in 'and so on'
G again, golf in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A golf addict plays round after round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'soundly' is a pun: the thing is beaten so that it sounds, not beaten decisively.
explanation.definitionFit: A gong is a metal disc struck with a beater to make a ringing noise.

clue.text: Bad boy keeps love in dump

parts.note: off means gone bad, as with milk

indicators.note: the boy keeps the love letter inside him

parts.note: a lad is a boy
love is nil in tennis, the letter O

explanation.surface: A naughty boy hides his sweetheart in a rubbish tip.
explanation.definitionFit: To get rid of something unwanted is to unload it onto someone or somewhere.

clue.text: Sage saw this could sum up HM's 50th anniversary

definitions.meaning: a wise saying, a maxim of conduct

definitions.text: this could sum up HM's 50th anniversary
definitions.meaning: a fiftieth anniversary is golden, and a monarch's reign is her rule, so HM's fifty years were a gold-standard reign

explanation.surface: A wise man said a single maxim summed up the Queen's golden jubilee.
explanation.walkthrough: HM is Her Majesty, the Queen; her Golden Jubilee in 2002 marked fifty years on the throne.
explanation.definitionFit: The best-known maxim is 'do as you would be done by', a guiding principle.

clue.text: Loose end to women's tennis match in east London?

indicators.note: in a Cockney accent of east London, th is said as f, so the phrase is heard with that sound

parts.note: women's tennis matches are best of three sets, so the last one is set three

explanation.surface: A women's tennis final reaches its deciding set somewhere in east London.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney speech, the dialect of east London, famously says 'free' for 'three'.
explanation.definitionFit: To loose a prisoner or animal is to release it, to let it go at liberty.

clue.text: First awarded to very loud university student — that's all one can grasp

indicators.note: the first place is handed to the very loud pair, sitting between its two letters

parts.note: FF is fortissimo, the musical marking for very loud
1ST, written with I for the figure one, is first
L, the learner plate, stands for a student

explanation.surface: A noisy undergraduate is given a first-class degree.

explanation.definitionFit: A fistful is a hand's capacity, the quantity a closed hand can hold.

clue.text: A1 to the south, Aunt Edna rambles past it

parts.note: A1 means first-rate, super

indicators.note: Aunt Edna rambles, so her letters wander into a new order

clue.text: Clumsy delivery by local hiding identity and lying

explanation.walkthrough: 'delivery' means manner of speaking, not a parcel brought to the door.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who keeps having mishaps through clumsiness is said to be liable to them in this way.

clue.text: Well I never joke over hosting company — one suppresses a lot

indicators.note: presses down on: in a down clue, the one sits on top of the a

parts.note: cor is a British exclamation of surprise

indicators.note: the reversed joke holds the company letters inside it
turned over, so the joke is reversed

parts.note: a pun is a joke
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A surprised reaction to a joke told over the firm's dinner, while one person holds back their laughter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' turns the joke backwards to NUP before 'hosting' wraps it round the company; COR is a British cry of surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: The horn of plenty symbolises abundance, so it can stand for a great amount.

clue.text: Unfashionable kind of fur's put by as best

parts.note: out means no longer in fashion
fox is a fur used in coats and stoles

explanation.surface: Fox fur, once prized, has gone out of fashion and is now stored away.
explanation.definitionFit: To best someone is to beat them, here by being more cunning than they are.

clue.text: Person taking time to break in, not so polite?

definitions.text: Person taking time to break in, not so polite?

indicators.note: the time letter breaks into the run made by the next two pieces, splitting it

parts.note: taken as written
ruder means less polite

explanation.surface: A burglar takes his time breaking in, and is ruder than a guest would be.
explanation.walkthrough: T breaks INRUDER after its second letter; read whole, the clue also describes a rude interloper.

clue.text: Scarf and angora used in dance? On the contrary

clue.text: All-round goalie's kept in African province and across the country

indicators.note: the goalie's number is kept inside the province's name

parts.note: Natal was a province of South Africa, now KwaZulu-Natal

indicators.note: turned all the way round, so the goalie's number is read backwards

parts.note: the goalkeeper wears number one, written NO I

explanation.surface: A goalkeeper famous in every part of a South African province.
explanation.walkthrough: A goalkeeper traditionally wears the number one shirt; 'All-round' turns NO I to ION before 'kept in' tucks it into the province.
explanation.definitionFit: Something nationwide reaches every part of a country, as with a national campaign.

clue.text: Draw Test, rolling a pitch to take spin

indicators.note: rolled over, so the test's letters are reversed

parts.note: the MOT is the annual UK roadworthiness test for vehicles

indicators.note: spun round, so these letters are read backwards

parts.note: to lob is to pitch, throw high

explanation.surface: A Test match groundsman rolls the pitch so it will take spin.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket Test and pitch hide a car test (MOT) and a throw.
explanation.definitionFit: A lottery where tickets are pulled from a drum for prizes is a kind of raffle.

clue.text: Mostly stationary after short distance — stopped halfway through drive home

indicators.note: the not-moving word comes after the halved distance
the short distance is cut off at its midpoint, keeping only its front half

parts.note: an inch is a short distance

indicators.note: most but not all of the word for not moving, so its last letter goes

parts.note: still means not moving

explanation.definitionFit: To drive home a point is to impress it firmly on someone's mind, gradually fixing it there.

clue.text: Chant repeatedly with tense accompaniment from this?

clue.text: US-made capsule that got its users high

clue.text: Not very nice after having caught nothing — two maidens, holding plenty
